title: Erin Levine — Hello Divorce: unbundling the divorce process for people priced out of lawyers
pub: Divorce & Beyond podcast (host Susan Guthrie), YouTube
author: Erin Levine

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Levine does not address AI’s jagged capabilities, selective deployment, verification or human–AI workflow design. She instead reframes legal-service transformation around a holistic, consumer-centred alternative to adversarial divorce, with industry disruption presented as an aspiration rather than evidence of AI-driven work redesign.

kp.k: Affordability motivated a broader redesign of divorce services
kp.d: Levine says Hello Divorce initially sought to provide a cheaper alternative to lawyers because 80% of people could not afford an attorney. She reports that interviews with hundreds of people, including those who received good legal advice, revealed dissatisfaction with the overall divorce experience. This prompted a broader effort to replace adversarial, opaque processes with support for the entire life transition. These are the founder's reported observations, not independently presented research findings.
qs: the goal early on was to build a cheaper alternative to a lawyer 80% of people could not afford an attorney
even after interviewing hundreds and hundreds of people that did have a lawyer and did receive good legal advice they weren't happy with their experience for the most part

kp.k: AI and automation accompany human case coordination
kp.d: Levine describes an AI chatbot, resources and calculators supporting couples who reach agreement themselves, alongside software automating legal and financial logistics. A human divorce specialist acts as project manager, checks forms, coordinates signatures, files documents and manages court responses through delivery of the signed divorce documents. The transcript does not provide separate measurements of the chatbot's performance or isolate AI's contribution to costs or outcomes.
qs: the parties are able to come to an agreement on their own with our resources and calculators our AI chatbot
software that automates all of the legal and financial Logistics
a divorce specialist who comes in and is a project manager is going to look at all your forms

going to coordinate signatures between you and your spouse going to deal with the court directly by filing the documents letting you know if the court has rejected it for any reason and needs an additional form

kp.k: Unbundling replaces exclusive reliance on a retained lawyer
kp.d: Levine recommends matching each problem to the appropriate professional: financial issues may warrant a certified divorce financial analyst, while legal issues warrant a lawyer. The platform offers optional access to mediators, lawyers and financial professionals, including short consultations, rather than requiring a substantial retainer and exclusive reliance on one professional. Customers may also combine its software and resources with outside experts.
qs: you can still use our software and still use our other services and resources
if it's a a legal issue then let's talk to a lawyer but we're no longer bound by having to pay a massive retainer and only work with one professional
it might make sense to use the platform to meet with a professional for 30 minutes or an hour
the goal is is for the platform to be flexible enough to bring in who you need when you need it

kp.k: Reported pricing combines software and optional professional assistance
kp.d: Levine reports an average divorce spend of $1,500, including users of a $400 software-only product. She says about 19% of customers need additional financial advice, legal advice or mediation; the transcript renders their combined spending range ambiguously as 'between 25 and 4500'. She also reports rare cases costing 'six seven $8,000' for both spouses in contested multimillion-dollar estates. These are provider-reported prices and spending figures, not a controlled comparison with traditional representation.
qs: the average divorce at hello divorce is $1,500
which is about 19% of our customers
you can expect to spend between 25 and 4500 total for both of you
we have had a rare occasion where both spouses total spent six seven $8,000
in General the average spend is 1,500 and and that also includes many people who use our $400 product which is just software only

kp.k: Affordable services still require support beyond DIY
kp.d: Drawing on helping over 6,000 people, Levine says most customers do not want a purely do-it-yourself process: unwillingness to pay large legal fees does not mean unwillingness to receive assistance. She identifies procedural complexity and bureaucracy as independent sources of difficulty, even apart from emotional and financial issues. Her argument supports a service model combining software with optional human assistance rather than software-only substitution.
qs: after now helping over 6,000 people I can tell you that DIY is really you know not what the vast majority of people want
just because people don't want to pay 203 $40,000 for a lawyer doesn't mean they don't want some support
even just taking out the emotion and the finances the procedure and the like Logistics the bureaucracy of it all is hard

kp.k: Local court procedures complicate geographic expansion
kp.d: Levine identifies differences between states, counties and individual courthouses in filing procedures, signatures and document preparation as obstacles to scaling the legal product. She distinguishes geographic expansion of that product from national expansion of Hello Next Chapter, its broader resource platform. The discussion concerns operational procedural variation, not a claim about changes to professional ownership or unauthorized-practice rules.
qs: the process is different in every single state
all of those things can sometimes differ County to County and sometimes Courthouse to courthouse
while expanding geographically with our legal product we've also begun to expand nationally with our what we call hello next chapter our platform that helps with additional resources

kp.k: Home Split integrates financial decisions with divorce execution
kp.d: Levine says Home Split was introduced and beta tested at the end of 2023, attracting 7200 users with little marketing. Its three steps estimate home equity and available options, connect users with a divorce real-estate expert, and help secure agreement and a transaction partner. It can be used before, during or after divorce, including by people using outside lawyers or mediators. She reports that 82% of married couples own homes and that at least one spouse wants to remain in the home in 90% of couples using Hello Divorce; the transcript provides no underlying datasets.
qs: we beta tested it at the end of 2023 to see if this would be something that people would be interested in and had 7200 people use it with very little marketing and advertising
82% of married couples own a home
the first step is to use a calculator
the second step is to hop on a call with a divorce real estate expert
the third step is to help you and your spouse get to that agreement
90% of the couples that use hello divorce at least one spouse wants to stay in the home

kp.k: Transaction commissions supplement paid divorce services
kp.d: Levine explains that Home Split's calculator, resources and real-estate expert call are free to consumers. Some vetted transaction partners pay a commission to Hello Divorce's real-estate subsidiary when a transaction closes. Additional mediation, financial advice, consultation with a customer's lawyer or legal-paperwork software can incur separate charges. This describes a revenue model extending beyond fees for legal work.
qs: all of that kind of stuff is free including the call
some of them if that transaction closes some of them pay our real estate subsidiary a commission to us directly
doesn't come out of your pocket but it's paid to us to our brokerage
the only time you would pay us out of pocket is if you get to step three and you and your spouse need some extra help coming to an agreement

kp.k: Conflict reduction is central, but litigation limits suitability
kp.d: Levine says the service is not necessarily suitable for an entire divorce if either spouse insists on litigating every issue. However, customers need not arrive amicable or already in agreement: she describes conflictual couples entering with at least one spouse seeking to stay out of court. Based on the provider's experience, she attributes much divorce conflict to fear and says the process deliberately creates incremental agreements to rebuild trust. These are experiential claims about service design, not demonstrated causal effects.
qs: it's not going to be the right fit for your entire divorce if both spouses or even one is determined to go to court for every little issue
many of them are not coming to the platform with an agreement
they are coming to the platform at least one of them with the goal of staying out of court
most of the conflict comes from fear
our entire process is designed to not just get your forms completed but help you and your spouse have some wins along the way

kp.k: Guided completion targets months rather than prolonged uncertainty
kp.d: Levine describes a three-step process intended to keep customers moving toward completion in six months or less, while noting that divorce cannot happen overnight. She reports an average marriage length of 13 years among platform customers and describes usual progress over roughly five to six months. Host Susan Guthrie separately contrasts this with her experience of litigated cases taking about a year in Connecticut and potentially years in California; the episode does not establish a comparable measured time saving.
qs: we have a three-step process we will keep you moving forward
wrap up your divorce in six months or less
on for our platform on average is 13 years
usually around you know five five six months
in Connecticut it was like a year for a litigated divorce

kp.k: Industry disruption is an access-oriented ambition
kp.d: Levine frames the long-term mission as disrupting what she calls the $50 billion-a-year family-law industry and changing expectations that divorce requires hiring lawyers and fighting. She presents affordable, holistic support as a way to avoid forcing people to remain in unhealthy relationships because they fear bankruptcy or for their safety. This is an access-to-justice and service-redesign ambition, not evidence that industry-wide transformation has occurred.
qs: nobody should ever have to stay in an unhappy or an unhealthy relationship just because they fear for their safety or bankruptcy
until the entire 50 billion doll year Family Law industry is disrupted and consumers no longer expect that divorce means lawyer up and fights
they trust that there's a holistic supportive Solution that's designed to help them transition into their next best chapter

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Erin Levine describes an AI chatbot as one component of Hello Divorce's lower-cost, supported divorce service, rather than claiming that AI independently replaces lawyers or handles an entire divorce.
pts.d: Levine says couples can reach agreement using the platform's resources, calculators and AI chatbot, with software automating legal and financial logistics and a human divorce specialist checking documents, coordinating signatures and managing court filings. She reports an average divorce cost of $1,500. This is a claim about the combined service: she does not isolate AI's contribution to costs, agreement rates or completion times, or specify the chatbot's capabilities. Her broader ambition to disrupt family law concerns the holistic service model, not an explicit prediction about AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Levine's operational experience and self-reported customer and pricing figures for Hello Divorce, not an AI-specific evaluation.
pts.d: Levine refers to helping over 6,000 people, reports a $1,500 average spend that includes software-only customers using a $400 product, and says approximately 19% of customers need additional financial, legal or mediation support. She also describes rare, higher-cost contested multimillion-dollar estates. These figures describe the overall platform; the interview provides no chatbot benchmark, accuracy measurement, comparative study or quantified attribution of savings to AI. Her observation that most users want some support also supplies an experience-based rationale for combining technology with professionals.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Levine describes an existing service in the 2024 interview, qualified by couples' ability or willingness to resolve issues outside court; she gives no AI-specific future adoption timeline.
pts.d: The $1,500 service description assumes parties can reach agreement using platform resources. Additional professional assistance is available for more complicated matters. Levine explicitly excludes cases where a spouse remains determined to litigate every issue from being a good fit for the entire divorce, while noting that initial conflict or threats of litigation do not necessarily preclude participation. She describes a five-to-six-month progression and a goal of completion in six months or less for the overall supported process, not an AI-caused speed improvement. She also notes state and local procedural variation and ongoing geographic expansion of the legal product.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The intended beneficiaries are divorcing individuals and couples, initially those priced out of lawyers, who receive technology-supported assistance with optional professional help.
pts.d: Levine says the initial purpose was affordable access to legal assistance for people unable to afford an attorney, later expanding to people who could afford lawyers but wanted a different experience. In the described model, clients use self-service resources including AI, a divorce specialist handles process administration and document checking, and lawyers, mediators and financial professionals provide targeted support when needed. The source does not predict AI-driven job losses or quantify changes in professional staffing. The relevant access-to-justice claim concerns individual divorce needs, not enterprise legal cost savings.
